title: Graceful degradation: fallback weave and rate-smoothing ops draft
content:
Summary:

This doc captures a working draft for how we want the stack to behave when Dedicated GPU pools degrade due to noisy tenants or autoscaler misconfig. Aim: define a lightweight, gradual graceful-degradation path (fallback weave) + rate-smoothing heuristics to avoid cascade evictions and to preserve SLOs for high-priority tenants. This is intentionally operational (commands, signals, quick checks) — not final policy.

Context / why now:
- Last three weekends we saw repeated midday throughput drops in pool-east-1-dedicated-2, correlated with a tenant generating large batched rerank jobs and another doing long context completions.
- Autoscaler misconfig (too-aggressive scale-down cooldown + hysteresis) amplified a transient IO pressure into a persistent capacity shortfall.
- Current fallback behavior is binary: either we evict or we do nothing. That binary decision led to either cascading evictions or expensive emergency scale-ups. We need intermediate graceful modes.

Observed signals (from the incident on 2025-10-27):
- 11:02 UTC: first latency tail increase; 95th token latency rose from 180ms to 360ms over 8 minutes.
- 11:10 UTC: allocator signaled memory pressure; KV cache hit rate for sharded-prefix route fell from 0.78 to 0.41.
- 11:14 UTC: autoscaler triggered scale-down rollback attempt incorrectly (cooldown windows overlapping) and later triggered an aggressive eviction at 11:22 UTC.
- 11:22 UTC: eviction caused 8 tenants to be rescheduled; two high-priority tenants (customer A + internal canary) saw request failures; fallback to CPU variant not configured for these tenants.

Hypotheses we tested during the incident (and quick results):
- Hypothesis A: Noisy tenant doing large batch reranks saturated GPU memory/KV cache causing cache amplification. Quick-test: pinned noisy tenant to a single GPU pool and replicated workload — reproduced transient spike.
- Hypothesis B: Autoscaler cooldown/hysteresis misconfig allowed a partial scale decision and later forced an eviction. Quick-check: autoscaler logs showed cooldown values of 3m during rolling updates; reducing to 60s prevented immediate eviction in repro.
- Hypothesis C: Lack of per-tenant soft-fallback meant high-priority traffic had no controlled degradation path. We simulated prefix-shed to lower-QPS and saw service continuity with longer latency but no failures.

Proposed graceful-degradation weave (sketch):
1) Signal tiers: define three signal levels for a pool: STABLE, PRESSURE, CRITICAL. Map telemetry thresholds to these (latency tail, memory free, KV hit drop, OOM count).
2) PRESSURE actions (fast, reversible):
   - Activate per-tenant rate-smoothing: short token-bucket throttles implemented at the gateway for low-priority routes (configurable per route).
   - Reduce batch size cap for new requests to preserve headroom (batch-size ceiling reduced by 30%).
   - Turn on expanded KV sharing (allow read-only KV sharing across compatible tenants temporarily) if supported by runtime.
3) CRITICAL actions (if PRESSURE persists > X minutes):
   - Start targeted soft-fallbacks: route selected classes of requests to lower-memory quantized model variant (auto-compatible list).
   - Prevent full eviction sweeps for Y minutes; instead do targeted drain for the top noisy tenant (identified by token emission rate and memory increase rate).
   - Trigger ops alert with recommended mitigation commands (see runbook snippet).

Rate-smoothing heuristics (gateway-level):
- Implement a sliding-window adaptive token-bucket per route where the rate cap is a function of pool free-memory and recent 95th latency. Example: cap = max( base_cap * (free_mem_pct / 0.6), min_cap ).
- Short-term burst allowance: allow a 10% burst above cap for 20s, then enforce backpressure for 2× the burst window.
- Prefer shedding low-priority non-interactive requests (batch inference / rerank / long-completion). Marked by header X-Request-Class.

Quick ops runbook (for on-call):
- Triage (first 10 minutes):
  1) Open incident channel and annotate pool id + time.
  2) Query allocator and serving metrics: allocator.free_mem_pct, pool.kv_hit_rate, pool.oom_count, per-tenant.token_rate.
     - kubectl logs allocator -n serving --since=15m | grep "pool-east-1-dedicated-2"
     - prometheus: sum by (tenant) (rate(tokens_emitted[1m]))
  3) If free_mem_pct < 35% OR kv_hit_rate < 0.5 -> label pool as PRESSURE.
- Immediate mitigations under PRESSURE (10–30 minutes):
  a) Apply rate-smoothing for low-priority routes: set gateway path /v1/embeddings batch route cap to 60% of normal.
     - gatewayctl apply-rate-cap --pool pool-east-1-dedicated-2 --route /v1/embeddings --cap 0.6
  b) Decrease new-request batch-size cap: runtimectl set-batch-ceiling --pool pool-east-1-dedicated-2 --factor 0.7
  c) If a single tenant accounts for >40% of token_rate and memory_growth_slope high -> soft-quarantine that tenant: move to ephemeral-quarantine pool if available.
- Escalation under CRITICAL (>30m unresolved):
  i) Apply targeted soft-fallbacks for high-latency routes: route to quantized-8bit variants by setting fallback-priority for tenant.
  ii) If fallback not possible, and failures likely: trigger scaled emergency expansion (dedicated-burst-cap) while ops coordinate long-term fix.
  iii) Avoid full eviction sweep unless OOM spikes > 5 in 10m. Eviction has high blast radius.

Runbook snippet: commands to run from on-call laptop:
- Check per-tenant token rate (1m windows):
  curl -s "https://prometheus/api/v1/query?query=sum%20by(tenant)(rate(tokens_emitted[1m]))" | jq .data.result
- Gate route caps:
  ssh gateway-admin@jump
  gatewayctl apply-rate-cap --pool pool-east-1-dedicated-2 --route /v1/completions --cap 0.5 --reason "mitigate-memory-pressure"
- Reduce batch ceiling:
  runtimectl set-batch-ceiling --pool pool-east-1-dedicated-2 --factor 0.7 --reason "pressure-mode"
- Soft-quarantine a tenant (manual, last resort):
  allocatorctl cordon-tenant --tenant-id tenant-xyz --target-pool pool-ephemeral-1 --drain-mode soft --note "noisy-tenant-2025-10-27"

Open questions / design decisions we need to resolve:
- How do we classify compatibility for soft-fallback model variants (schema, function-calling differences)? Need a model-compatibility manifest per model.
- Unsafe to enable KV sharing across tenants broadly — need proof-of-concept and security signoff.
- Cooldown tuning: experiment with 60s vs 120s for scale-down windows in practice; adjust by pool size.
- SLO prioritization: agree on what traffic is "high-priority" for rollback/exemptions. Current proposal: customers with reserved SLA tags + internal canaries.

Post-incident action items (owners & rough ETA):
- Diego Morales: prototype gateway rate-smoothing plugin + basic autopilot for free_mem_pct -> cap (ETA 2w).
- Chen Li: add model-compatibility manifest prototype and small API to list fallback-compatible variants (ETA 3w).
- Riley Thompson: run controlled chaos experiments in canary region to test PRESSURE->CRITICAL transitions (ETA 2 weeks).
- Aisha Patel (me): write an expanded playbook with concrete thresholds, add to oncall checklist; schedule review with runtime / product (ETA 1 week).

Notes from on-call chat (raw snippets):
- Riley: "saw the OOM count spike right before the allocator log; suspected KV blowout"
- Diego: "if we can throttle rerank qps quickly we avoid eviction 90% of the time in repro"
- Chen: "even a 30% batch size cap yields 15–20% more free mem headroom in our sim"

Appendix: lightweight experiment plan (to validate key parts)
1) Canary: deploy rate-smoothing in pool-canary-1, slowly increase synthetic rerank QPS until we see PRESSURE thresholds, measure incident delta vs baseline.
2) Fallback simulation: add small client-side shim to route to quantized variant when flagged, measure quality regression and cost delta.
3) Autoscaler cooldown test: run A/B with 60s and 180s cooldowns and measure eviction counts for transient load bursts.

If you're reading this and have operational experience with similar fallback patterns, please add notes below or ping me directly. This needs cross-team validation (runtime, allocator, gateway, product).

-- Aisha
